Nope. That's your bullet naming conventions, right there: a reference to the diameter of the bullet in inches or millimeters is its caliber. Rifled barrels make this a bit more complicated, and the number is only approximate.

What we have here is a shot gun. Note that OP said it was "capable of killing 50 birds at once". I suppose, technically, any shell with more than 50 pieces of shot (more a function of shot size, than anything) could do that, if you were very lucky, but this gun had a good chance at it. Shotguns are measured by the diameter of the barrel in "gauges". The 12-gauge is the worlds most popular shotgun, but there is also a 36-gauge. It's smaller. (Americans call it the .410, like rifles.) Bigger numbers mean smaller guns? What madness is this? The gauge should have a diameter of it's inverse in a pound of lead. That is, a 12 gauge should have a barrel wide enough to accommodate a ball of lead weighing 1/12 pound.

This bad boy? 0 or 00 gauge. They shot more than a pound of lead at a time. Imagine the recoil! To help with that, they were mounted on "punts". Hence, the name.

Edit to add: if bullet naming conventions were applied, this thing would be closer to the 1.88 magnum.
